planting.note: Set divisions or container plants out after all danger of frost in humusy, moist, well-drained soil in dappled or partial shade; this Brazilian relative of spiderwort is not frost tolerant, so Gulf Coast gardeners outside the warmest microclimates should grow it in a large container that can be moved under cover in hard freezes.

directions: Despite the common name, this is a Commelinaceae relative of spiderwort, not a true ginger, grown for its glossy cane-like stems and pendulous spikes of small cobalt-blue flowers produced nearly year-round. Site it in a sheltered, humidity-retaining spot with filtered light beneath larger shrubs or a porch overhang, since the thin leaves scorch in direct summer sun but the plant still needs bright, open shade to flower well. Top-prune the upright canes periodically to keep clumps bushy and encourage branching, and propagate easily by cutting sections of cane or by dividing crowded clumps in spring. In zone 9a gardens it is best treated as a root-hardy perennial that may die back to the crown in a cold winter, resprouting from below ground once soil warms.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension -- Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to part sun; space 4-5 feet apart center-to-center for a solid hedge or screen.

directions: Moonlit Lace is a Viburnum tinus x Viburnum davidii hybrid first discovered at a specialty Japanese nursery and now distributed in the US by Nurseries Caroliniana; it combines the glossy, leathery, red-tinted new foliage and compact mounding habit of V. davidii with the heat tolerance and lacy white spring flower clusters of V. tinus, solving V. davidii's tendency to decline in the humid Southeast. Site it in bright, open, partial shade such as a woodland edge or the north side of a building, since it tolerates more shade than most flowering viburnums but still blooms best with some filtered sun. Mulch well to conserve moisture, water weekly while establishing, and prune lightly right after bloom to maintain a tidy rounded form. It makes an excellent lower-growing informal hedge or foundation shrub where bulkier viburnums would overwhelm the space.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; space 4 feet apart center-to-center for a hedge or screen, or 7 feet apart for specimen and mass plantings.

directions: Juliet is a patented Southern Living Plant Collection selection of Ternstroemia gymnanthera (commonly sold as 'cleyera' though a different genus from true Cleyera japonica) prized for olive-green leaves broadly edged in creamy white, with new growth emerging maroon before settling into its variegated mature color. It tolerates considerably more shade than most broadleaf screening shrubs, making it useful as a bright privacy hedge along a partially shaded fence line or under high pine canopy where glossy green hollies and photinias thin out. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer in spring and prune right before new growth emerges in late winter to maintain density, since it blooms on new wood with small, inconspicuous white flowers that are not the main ornamental feature. It is notably heat and humidity tolerant and largely free of the disease pressure that plagues red-tip photinia in Gulf Coast gardens.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall 1-2 inches above grade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil with morning sun and afternoon shade; mulch to keep roots cool and consistently moist through Gulf Coast summer heat.

directions: Cherry Explosion is a Southern Living Plant Collection lacecap bigleaf hydrangea, patented in 2017, with bold cherry-red outer florets surrounding shell-pink centers, reblooming from mid-spring into fall on a compact, 3-foot-by-3-foot frame that fits smaller shade-garden beds better than older full-size mopheads. Give it a spot with gentle morning sun and reliable afternoon shade, since full-day Gulf Coast sun will scorch the leaves and stress the plant even with ample water. Flower color shifts toward lavender-pink in acidic soils and stays truer red-pink as soil pH rises, so gardeners can nudge the color with soil amendments. Fertilize each spring and prune only right after flowering concludes, since old wood carries next year's buds.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; like other Indian pink selections it resents root disturbance once established, so choose a permanent site at planting time.

directions: Orange Slices is a 2026 Proven Winners introduction of the Gulf Coast native woodland wildflower Indian pink, selected for richer red-and-orange bicolor tubular flowers held above tidy clumping foliage from late spring into early summer. It is one of the best true hummingbird plants for a shaded border, performing happily from full sun to fairly deep shade as long as soil stays evenly moist and rich in organic matter. Clumps are slow to bulk up for the first year or two after transplanting but become long-lived and reliably floriferous once settled, and the self-cleaning flowers need no deadheading. Combine it with woodland phlox, native sedges, and ferns for a layered native shade planting that draws pollinators through the heat of summer.
